flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the back legs' mortises, 3/16" longer toward the back, leave the top room to move against tenons glued at the front.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the 5" of top past the legs at each end carries heavy work there, such as chopping or work held in the end vise.
flags.why: Kerf computes only the top’s sag between the legs, not what it carries past them.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether screws for the upper drawers’ slides, driven into both faces of the divider at the same height, will meet inside it.
flags.why: Screws longer than half the divider’s 3/4" meet in the middle when the holes line up. Staggering the two slides’ holes, or shorter screws, avoids it.

assumptions: All of it sits at the middle of the span, where the top bends most.
The top runs past the legs and is held by their tenons; taking it as simply supported overstates its deflection.
The dog holes and the mortises take a little out of the section and are left out, which understates it slightly.
Simply supported between the two supports.
E is the average for small, clear, straight-grained specimens; boards with knots or cross grain may be less stiff.
E includes shear deflection, so bending deflection alone is computed.
E is at 12% moisture content; most properties increase as wood dries below that, so drier indoor wood is stiffer.
No NDS adjustment factors apply to a clear-wood value.

checklist.element: The base: legs, feet, and rails
checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the glued mortises and tenons keep the base square and steady when planing pushes the top along and across.
checklist.why: Hand planing pushes hard on a bench, and Kerf does not compute joint strength.

checklist.element: The bench with a vise open
checklist.confirm: Confirm whether the bench can tip when planing at an end past the legs, or with work in an open vise.
checklist.why: The top runs past the legs at each end, and a vise holds work farther out still.

checklist.element: The through tenons and the back mortises
checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder how much glue the front tenons through the top need, and that the back tenons stay unglued in their long mortises.
checklist.why: The top holds the frame together at its tenons, and gluing the back ones would stop it moving.

checklist.element: Glue lines in the top and legs
checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the strips of the top and legs are glued well enough for heavy work.
checklist.why: Kerf does not compute the strength of glue lines.

checklist.element: Bending and shear of the top
checklist.confirm: Confirm the top is strong enough, not only stiff enough.
checklist.why: There are no published design values for furniture lumber, so Kerf checks only deflection.

checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the dovetailed boxes suit what goes in them.
checklist.why: Tools are heavy, and Kerf computes nothing for the drawers.

steps.title: Let the lumber settle indoors

method.name: Stacked and left to settle
setup: Bring the boards into the room where the piece will stand, or a heated room like it, as soon as you buy them.
technique: Stack the boards flat with thin, dry strips of wood across them every foot or two, so air reaches every face.
Leave them for a couple of weeks before cutting, longer for boards that felt cool or damp at the store or that were stored outside.
mistakes: Gluing up boards that are still drying leaves them to shrink in the panel, which can open the joints or crack it. Give them time indoors first.
Stacking boards flat on each other traps moisture between them. Put strips between every layer.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the preservative in your treated lumber calls for more than a dust mask, gloves, and washing up when you sand it.
flags.why: Breathing wood dust can cause allergic and other respiratory symptoms, and dust from treated wood carries the preservative.

steps.title: Finish

alternatives.methodName: Sanded by hand, then wiped on

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder which finish suits the wood and where it will stand, and follow the product's instructions for ventilation.
flags.why: Rags wet with oil-based finish can catch fire on their own. Store them in a tightly sealed metal container, then throw them away.

steps.title: Let the lumber settle indoors

method.name: Stacked and left to settle
setup: Bring the boards into the room where the piece will stand, or a heated room like it, as soon as you buy them.
technique: Stack the boards flat with thin, dry strips of wood across them every foot or two, so air reaches every face.
Leave them for a couple of weeks before cutting, longer for boards that felt cool or damp at the store or that were stored outside.
mistakes: Gluing up boards that are still drying leaves them to shrink in the panel, which can open the joints or crack it. Give them time indoors first.
Stacking boards flat on each other traps moisture between them. Put strips between every layer.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the back legs' mortises, 3/16" longer toward the back, leave the top room to move against tenons glued at the front.
flags.why: The top moves across its 17-5/8" depth with the seasons, and the legs' tenons go through it 13-5/8" apart. The Wood Movement section estimates how much.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the 5" of top past the legs at each end carries heavy work there, such as chopping or work held in the end vise.
flags.why: Kerf computes only the top’s sag between the legs, not what it carries past them.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether screws for the upper drawers’ slides, driven into both faces of the divider at the same height, will meet inside it.
flags.why: Screws longer than half the divider’s 3/4" meet in the middle when the holes line up. Staggering the two slides’ holes, or shorter screws, avoids it.

steps.title: Cut board 1, a 13/16" x 5-1/2" 10' long: Top board for strips, Low rail board for strips

method.name: With a miter saw
setup: Set the miter saw square, with no miter and no bevel.
Support the board level with the saw table on both sides of the blade.
technique: Mark the length on the board.
Hold the board against the fence, with the blade on the waste side of the mark.
Let the blade reach full speed, then lower it through the board.
Let the blade stop before you raise it.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Cutting on the mark makes the part short by the width of the blade. Put the blade on the waste side of the mark.

safety.text: Keep the blade guard on and working: it must cover the blade whenever the blade is not in the wood.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

technique: Mark the length on the board.
Hold the board against the fence, with the blade on the waste side of the mark.
Let the blade reach full speed, then lower it through the board.
Let the blade stop before you raise it.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Cutting on the mark makes the part short by the width of the blade. Put the blade on the waste side of the mark.

safety.text: Keep the blade guard on and working: it must cover the blade whenever the blade is not in the wood.

steps.title: Glue up the top, legs, and rails from strips

alternatives.methodName: With a band saw and a fence

method.name: In sections, with clamps and cauls
setup: Lay the 23 strips out in order, turned so the faces that meet are flat and clean, and mark a line across them so they go back the same way.
Clamp them dry to check that every glue line closes along its length with light pressure, and open the clamps past 18-11/16".
Cut straight scrap boards for cauls, as long as the glue-up is wide.
technique: Glue a few strips at a time into sections: spread glue evenly on every face that meets another, bring them together, and clamp them.

Put clamps along the length close enough together that a small bead of glue squeezes out along every glue line, alternating them on the two faces that show the strips’ edges, and clamp cauls across to hold the strips level.
Once a section’s glue holds, scrape off the squeeze-out on its faces, then glue the sections together the same way.
Leave the last glue-up clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
Glue up 1 this way.
mistakes: Spreading glue on every strip at once can take so long that the first faces dry before the clamps go on, and dried glue does not wet the other face. A section of a few strips goes together before that.
Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Strips that slip out of level leave a step on the edge faces deeper than flattening takes off. Keep the cauls tight and check each glue line with your fingers before the final tightening.

steps.title: Glue up the panels

method.name: With clamps and cauls
setup: Lay the 4 boards out in order with your marks lined up, and clamp them dry to check that every joint closes along its length with light pressure.
Open the clamps past 21-5/8", and cut straight scrap boards for cauls, as long as the panel is wide.
technique: Spread glue evenly along every glued edge.
Bring the boards together and put clamps across the panel, alternating above and below it.
Clamp a caul across each end of the panel, on both faces, to hold the boards level with each other.
Tighten the clamps evenly until a small bead of glue squeezes out along each joint.
Leave the panel clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
Glue up 1 this way.
mistakes: Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Using clamp pressure to close a gap leaves a thick, weak glue line. Joint the edges again until they meet along their length.
Glue left to skin over before the boards go together does not wet the other edge. Have everything ready before you spread the glue.

method.name: With a sander
setup: Let the panel rest for several days after glue-up, so the wood along the joints dries back before you sand it.
Scrape off the dried glue on both faces, and clamp the panel flat to the bench.
technique: Sand across each joint until the faces are level, then sand the whole face with the grain.
Check with a straightedge laid across the 21-5/8" panel as you go. Stop once it touches everywhere: the panel should still be at least 3/4" thick.
Flatten 1 this way.
mistakes: Holding the sander on a joint digs a hollow beside it. Keep the sander moving over a wide area.

safety.text: Breathing wood dust can cause respiratory symptoms. Wear a dust mask while you sand, and sweep up the dust rather than blowing it.
Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

method.name: With clamps and cauls
setup: Lay the 4 boards out in order with your marks lined up, and clamp them dry to check that every joint closes along its length with light pressure.
Open the clamps past 21-5/8", and cut straight scrap boards for cauls, as long as the panel is wide.
technique: Spread glue evenly along every glued edge.
Bring the boards together and put clamps across the panel, alternating above and below it.
Clamp a caul across each end of the panel, on both faces, to hold the boards level with each other.
Tighten the clamps evenly until a small bead of glue squeezes out along each joint.
Leave the panel clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
Glue up 1 this way.
mistakes: Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Using clamp pressure to close a gap leaves a thick, weak glue line. Joint the edges again until they meet along their length.
Glue left to skin over before the boards go together does not wet the other edge. Have everything ready before you spread the glue.

method.name: With a sander
setup: Let the panel rest for several days after glue-up, so the wood along the joints dries back before you sand it.
Scrape off the dried glue on both faces, and clamp the panel flat to the bench.
technique: Sand across each joint until the faces are level, then sand the whole face with the grain.
Check with a straightedge laid across the 21-5/8" panel as you go. Stop once it touches everywhere: the panel should still be at least 3/4" thick.
Flatten 1 this way.
mistakes: Holding the sander on a joint digs a hollow beside it. Keep the sander moving over a wide area.

safety.text: Breathing wood dust can cause respiratory symptoms. Wear a dust mask while you sand, and sweep up the dust rather than blowing it.
Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

anyOf: Circular saw with depth of cut with the blade square at least 2-1/2" (you entered 2-3/8")

method.name: With a circular saw, from two faces
setup: Set the blade as deep as it goes.
Support the board on sawhorses or blocks on both sides of the cut, and clamp it.
technique: Mark the length and square the line around all four faces.
Cut along the line on one face, with the blade on the waste side.
Turn the board over and cut along the line on the opposite face, so the two kerfs meet.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Lines that do not meet at the corners leave a step where the two cuts meet. Square every line from the same edge and face, and check that the last line meets the first.

safety.text: A circular saw kicks back toward you when the blade pinches in the cut. Support the board and both pieces of it, so neither drops into the blade as the cut finishes, and keep your hands out of the line of the cut.

setup: Set the miter saw square, with no miter and no bevel.
Support the board level with the saw table on both sides of the blade.
technique: Mark the length on the board.
Hold the board against the fence, with the blade on the waste side of the mark.
Let the blade reach full speed, then lower it through the board.
Let the blade stop before you raise it.
Cut 2 this way.
mistakes: Cutting on the mark makes the part short by the width of the blade. Put the blade on the waste side of the mark.

method.name: With a circular saw and a straight guide
setup: Set the blade a little deeper than the board is thick, 3/4".
Support the board on both sides of the cut and clamp it.
technique: Mark 16-5/8" from the edge kept at both ends, and join the marks with a line.
Clamp a straight board along the line as a guide, set back by the distance from the blade to the edge of the saw base.
Keep the base tight to the guide and cut the full 47-7/8".
Rip 1 this way.
mistakes: A guide that is not straight puts its curve in the part. Sight along the guide board, or use a factory edge.

safety.text: A circular saw kicks back toward you when the blade pinches in the cut. Support the board and both pieces of it, so neither drops into the blade as the cut finishes, and keep your hands out of the line of the cut.

steps.title: Cut the mortises

method.name: With a drill and a chisel

tools.use: a bit as wide as the mortise

setup: Mark the mortise on the part: 2-1/2" long and 1" wide, where the cut detail shows it.
Fit a bit 1" across, and mark it or set a stop for 2-1/2" deep.
Clamp the part flat, with the marked side up.
technique: Drill a row of holes inside the marks, each 2-1/2" deep, overlapping a little.
Pare the walls to the marks with the chisel, its flat side toward the wall and held upright.
Clean the bottom with the chisel until it is flat at 2-1/2" all along.
Check the fit with the tenon it holds, and pare where it binds.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Drilling at a lean makes the mortise wider at the bottom or out of line. Keep the bit upright, checking from two sides.
Prying with the chisel against a wall crushes the edge. Pare a little at a time, and lever only on the waste.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

Clamp the part flat, with the marked side up.
technique: Drill a row of holes inside the marks, each 2-1/2" deep, overlapping a little.
Pare the walls to the marks with the chisel, its flat side toward the wall and held upright.
Clean the bottom with the chisel until it is flat at 2-1/2" all along.
Check the fit with the tenon it holds, and pare where it binds.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Drilling at a lean makes the mortise wider at the bottom or out of line. Keep the bit upright, checking from two sides.

steps.title: Bore the hinge cups and drill the screw holes

method.name: With a drill/driver

tools.use: drilling pilot holes and driving the screws

setup: Mark each plate’s screw holes on the face from the cut detail.
Chuck a bit for the pilot holes, the size the hinge’s maker says for the plate’s screws.
technique: Drill a pilot hole at each mark, as deep as the screws go.
Set a plate on its marks the way the maker’s diagram shows, and drive its 2 screws until each head is snug.
Screw on 2 plates this way.
mistakes: A screw driven at full speed strips its hole in the side, and the plate works loose. Set the clutch low and drive the last turns slowly.
Setting a plate turned around puts the hinge’s arm on the wrong side. Check it against the maker’s diagram before driving.

safety.text: Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

suggestions.methodName: With a drill and an impact driver

method.name: With a drill
setup: Mark each hole where the cut detail shows it, and which ones are slots.
Fit a bit the screw slides through without threading into the wood: its clearance hole, as the screw maker gives it.
Clamp the part flat on scrap, so the bit comes out clean.
technique: Drill 2 round holes straight through the 1/2" part.
For each of the 0 slots, drill the first hole, then a second 0" beyond it the way the slot runs, and holes between them so they overlap.
Pare the sides of each slot straight with the chisel, so the screw slides from one end to the other.
Drill 2 this way.
mistakes: A slot run the wrong way stops the part from moving, which can split it. Check which way each slot runs before you drill.
Driving a screw in a slot tight pins the part. Turn it until it is snug, so its head can still slide.

setup: Mark each hole where the cut detail shows it, and which ones are slots.
Fit a bit the screw slides through without threading into the wood: its clearance hole, as the screw maker gives it.
Clamp the part flat on scrap, so the bit comes out clean.
technique: Drill 0 round holes straight through the 1/2" part.
For each of the 1 slots, drill the first hole, then a second 3/16" beyond it the way the slot runs, and holes between them so they overlap.
Pare the sides of each slot straight with the chisel, so the screw slides from one end to the other.
Drill 1 this way.
mistakes: A slot run the wrong way stops the part from moving, which can split it. Check which way each slot runs before you drill.
Driving a screw in a slot tight pins the part. Turn it until it is snug, so its head can still slide.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

steps.title: Fit the bench together dry

method.name: Without clamps
setup: Clear a flat surface big enough for the whole assembly, and have someone help hold the parts.
Lay the parts out in the order they go together, each with its marks facing the way the plan shows.
technique: Put the parts together without glue, sliding each one into its dadoes.
Push each joint closed by hand and look for a gap.
Measure both diagonals of the front. When they match, the assembly is square.
Mark where each part meets its neighbors, so it goes back the same way, then take it apart.
mistakes: Forcing a tight joint together dry can split a part or leave it stuck. Stop, take it apart, and widen the dado a little.
A joint held closed by hand can hide a gap that clamps would show. Check each one while it is pushed fully home.

anyOf: Clamps with widest opening at least 61-7/8" (you entered 24")

steps.title: Glue up the end frames

method.name: With clamps
setup: Dry-fit the assembly first, and have every part and clamp within reach: the glue starts to dry as soon as it is spread.
Open the clamps past 18-5/8", and cut scrap pads to go under the jaws so they do not dent the faces.
technique: Spread a thin, even coat of glue in each dado and on the part that goes into it.
Slide each part into its dadoes, and clamp across the assembly over each joint.
Tighten the clamps evenly until a small bead of glue squeezes out at each joint.
Measure both diagonals. If they differ, angle a clamp along the longer one and tighten it until they match.
Scrape off the squeezed-out glue once it turns rubbery, so it does not keep the finish out.
Leave the assembly clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
mistakes: Glue spread long before the parts go together dries on the wood and makes a thick, weak joint. Spread it on one joint group at a time and close it right away.
Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Taking the clamps off early lets the joints shift or open. Leave them on for as long as the glue maker says.

steps.title: Fit the drawer bottoms and fronts

method.name: With a drill/driver
setup: Set the parts in place and clamp them so they cannot shift while you drive the screws.
Set the driver’s clutch low, so it slips before a screw goes in too far.
technique: Drive each of the 9 screws through its hole until the head is snug against the wood.
Leave the screws in slots snug, not tight, so the part they hold can still slide.
mistakes: Driving a screw in a slot tight pins the part, which can split it as it moves. Stop when the head is snug.
A screw driven at full speed strips its hole. Drive the last turns slowly.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

alternatives.methodName: With a drill press and its depth stop

anyOf: Drill press with column to the center of the bit at least 2" and deepest hole in one stroke at least 2-1/4"
Forstner bits with deepest hole from one side at least 2-1/4"

method.name: With a drill, from one side
setup: Mark each hole center from the cut detail on the side you bore from.
Chuck a 3/4" bit, and clamp a scrap board tight under the part where the bit comes out.
technique: Stand a square on the part beside the bit, and bore through the 2-1/2" of wood, checking square from two directions as the bit starts.
Back the bit out every inch or so to clear the chips.
Bore 1 holes this way.
mistakes: Letting the drill tilt puts the hole off square, so what stands in it leans. Check square from two directions as the bit starts, and again halfway.
Pushing the bit out through the far face with nothing behind it tears out the wood around the hole. Clamp a scrap board tight behind it.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

steps.title: Ease the edges

method.name: With a sander
setup: Clamp the part flat, or hold it on a bench against a stop.
technique: Sand each long edge with the sander tilted, rolling it over the corner until the corner is round.
Round the corners at each end the same way.
Sand every face a hand can touch until no splinter catches on a rag drawn across it.
Ease 1 this way.
mistakes: Holding the sander in one place on an edge cuts a flat or a dip. Keep it moving along the whole edge.

safety.text: Breathing wood dust can cause respiratory symptoms. Wear a dust mask while you sand, and sweep up the dust rather than blowing it.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the preservative in your treated lumber calls for more than a dust mask, gloves, and washing up when you sand it.
flags.why: Breathing wood dust can cause allergic and other respiratory symptoms, and dust from treated wood carries the preservative.

steps.title: Finish

method.name: Sanded, then wiped on
setup: Choose the finish with an experienced builder, and read its instructions for coats, drying time, and ventilation.
Work where fresh air moves through, away from flames and heat.
technique: Sand every face a person can see or touch, with the grain, ending with finer paper than you started with.
Vacuum the dust, then wipe the faces with a clean cloth.
Wipe on a thin coat with a clean rag, then wipe off what has not soaked in, as the instructions say.
Let it dry as long as the instructions say, sand lightly with fine paper, and add as many coats as they call for.
mistakes: Sanding across the grain leaves scratches that the finish makes stand out. Sand with the grain.
A thick coat dries soft and sticky. Wipe on thin coats and wipe off the excess.

safety.text: Rags wet with oil-based finish can catch fire on their own. Store them in a tightly sealed metal container, then throw them away.

hardwareNotes: The base is glued for good: the legs’ tenons into the feet and through the top, and the rails’ into the legs. The back legs’ tenons go unglued in their long mortises so the top can move.
The case back, door panels, and drawer bottoms float in their grooves, unglued.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the back legs' mortises, 1/4" longer toward the back, leave the top room to move against tenons glued at the front.
flags.why: The top moves across its 17-5/8" depth with the seasons, and the legs' tenons go through it 13-5/8" apart. The Wood Movement section estimates how much.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the 5" of top past the legs at each end carries heavy work there, such as chopping or work held in the end vise.
flags.why: Kerf computes only the top’s sag between the legs, not what it carries past them.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether screws for the upper drawers’ slides, driven into both faces of the divider at the same height, will meet inside it.
flags.why: Screws longer than half the divider’s 3/4" meet in the middle when the holes line up. Staggering the two slides’ holes, or shorter screws, avoids it.

checks.subject: Top
checks.loadCase: Everything on the bench at the middle of its span, for years

movement.subject: Top, between its front and back tenons

checklist.element: The base: legs, feet, and rails
checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the glued mortises and tenons keep the base square and steady when planing pushes the top along and across.
checklist.why: Hand planing pushes hard on a bench, and Kerf does not compute joint strength.

checklist.element: The bench with a vise open
checklist.confirm: Confirm whether the bench can tip when planing at an end past the legs, or with work in an open vise.
checklist.why: The top runs past the legs at each end, and a vise holds work farther out still.

checklist.element: The through tenons and the back mortises
checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder how much glue the front tenons through the top need, and that the back tenons stay unglued in their long mortises.
checklist.why: The top holds the frame together at its tenons, and gluing the back ones would stop it moving.

checklist.element: Glue lines in the top and legs
checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the strips of the top and legs are glued well enough for heavy work.
checklist.why: Kerf does not compute the strength of glue lines.

checklist.element: Bending and shear of the top
checklist.confirm: Confirm the top is strong enough, not only stiff enough.
checklist.why: There are no published design values for furniture lumber, so Kerf checks only deflection.

checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the dovetailed boxes suit what goes in them.
checklist.why: Tools are heavy, and Kerf computes nothing for the drawers.

steps.title: Let the lumber settle indoors

method.name: Stacked and left to settle
setup: Bring the boards into the room where the piece will stand, or a heated room like it, as soon as you buy them.
technique: Stack the boards flat with thin, dry strips of wood across them every foot or two, so air reaches every face.
Leave them for a couple of weeks before cutting, longer for boards that felt cool or damp at the store or that were stored outside.
mistakes: Gluing up boards that are still drying leaves them to shrink in the panel, which can open the joints or crack it. Give them time indoors first.
Stacking boards flat on each other traps moisture between them. Put strips between every layer.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the preservative in your treated lumber calls for more than a dust mask, gloves, and washing up when you sand it.
flags.why: Breathing wood dust can cause allergic and other respiratory symptoms, and dust from treated wood carries the preservative.

steps.title: Finish

alternatives.methodName: Sanded by hand, then wiped on

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder which finish suits the wood and where it will stand, and follow the product's instructions for ventilation.
flags.why: Rags wet with oil-based finish can catch fire on their own. Store them in a tightly sealed metal container, then throw them away.

steps.title: Let the lumber settle indoors

method.name: Stacked and left to settle
setup: Bring the boards into the room where the piece will stand, or a heated room like it, as soon as you buy them.
technique: Stack the boards flat with thin, dry strips of wood across them every foot or two, so air reaches every face.
Leave them for a couple of weeks before cutting, longer for boards that felt cool or damp at the store or that were stored outside.
mistakes: Gluing up boards that are still drying leaves them to shrink in the panel, which can open the joints or crack it. Give them time indoors first.
Stacking boards flat on each other traps moisture between them. Put strips between every layer.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the back legs' mortises, 1/4" longer toward the back, leave the top room to move against tenons glued at the front.
flags.why: The top moves across its 17-5/8" depth with the seasons, and the legs' tenons go through it 13-5/8" apart. The Wood Movement section estimates how much.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the 5" of top past the legs at each end carries heavy work there, such as chopping or work held in the end vise.
flags.why: Kerf computes only the top’s sag between the legs, not what it carries past them.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether screws for the upper drawers’ slides, driven into both faces of the divider at the same height, will meet inside it.
flags.why: Screws longer than half the divider’s 3/4" meet in the middle when the holes line up. Staggering the two slides’ holes, or shorter screws, avoids it.

steps.title: Cut board 1, a 13/16" x 5-1/2" 10' long: Top board for strips, Low rail board for strips

method.name: With a miter saw
setup: Set the miter saw square, with no miter and no bevel.
Support the board level with the saw table on both sides of the blade.
technique: Mark the length on the board.
Hold the board against the fence, with the blade on the waste side of the mark.
Let the blade reach full speed, then lower it through the board.
Let the blade stop before you raise it.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Cutting on the mark makes the part short by the width of the blade. Put the blade on the waste side of the mark.

safety.text: Keep the blade guard on and working: it must cover the blade whenever the blade is not in the wood.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

Support the board level with the saw table on both sides of the blade.
technique: Mark the length on the board.
Hold the board against the fence, with the blade on the waste side of the mark.
Let the blade reach full speed, then lower it through the board.
Let the blade stop before you raise it.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Cutting on the mark makes the part short by the width of the blade. Put the blade on the waste side of the mark.

safety.text: Keep the blade guard on and working: it must cover the blade whenever the blade is not in the wood.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

steps.title: Glue up the top, legs, and rails from strips

alternatives.methodName: With a band saw and a fence

method.name: In sections, with clamps and cauls
setup: Lay the 23 strips out in order, turned so the faces that meet are flat and clean, and mark a line across them so they go back the same way.
Clamp them dry to check that every glue line closes along its length with light pressure, and open the clamps past 18-11/16".
Cut straight scrap boards for cauls, as long as the glue-up is wide.
technique: Glue a few strips at a time into sections: spread glue evenly on every face that meets another, bring them together, and clamp them.

Put clamps along the length close enough together that a small bead of glue squeezes out along every glue line, alternating them on the two faces that show the strips’ edges, and clamp cauls across to hold the strips level.
Once a section’s glue holds, scrape off the squeeze-out on its faces, then glue the sections together the same way.
Leave the last glue-up clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
Glue up 1 this way.
mistakes: Spreading glue on every strip at once can take so long that the first faces dry before the clamps go on, and dried glue does not wet the other face. A section of a few strips goes together before that.
Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Strips that slip out of level leave a step on the edge faces deeper than flattening takes off. Keep the cauls tight and check each glue line with your fingers before the final tightening.

anyOf: Thickness planer with widest board at least 18-11/16"

Once a section’s glue holds, scrape off the squeeze-out on its faces, then glue the sections together the same way.
Leave the last glue-up clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
Glue up 2 this way.
mistakes: Spreading glue on every strip at once can take so long that the first faces dry before the clamps go on, and dried glue does not wet the other face. A section of a few strips goes together before that.
Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Strips that slip out of level leave a step on the edge faces deeper than flattening takes off. Keep the cauls tight and check each glue line with your fingers before the final tightening.

steps.title: Glue up the panels

method.name: With clamps and cauls
setup: Lay the 4 boards out in order with your marks lined up, and clamp them dry to check that every joint closes along its length with light pressure.
Open the clamps past 21-5/8", and cut straight scrap boards for cauls, as long as the panel is wide.
technique: Spread glue evenly along every glued edge.
Bring the boards together and put clamps across the panel, alternating above and below it.
Clamp a caul across each end of the panel, on both faces, to hold the boards level with each other.
Tighten the clamps evenly until a small bead of glue squeezes out along each joint.
Leave the panel clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
Glue up 1 this way.
mistakes: Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Using clamp pressure to close a gap leaves a thick, weak glue line. Joint the edges again until they meet along their length.
Glue left to skin over before the boards go together does not wet the other edge. Have everything ready before you spread the glue.

method.name: With a sander
setup: Let the panel rest for several days after glue-up, so the wood along the joints dries back before you sand it.
Scrape off the dried glue on both faces, and clamp the panel flat to the bench.
technique: Sand across each joint until the faces are level, then sand the whole face with the grain.
Check with a straightedge laid across the 21-5/8" panel as you go. Stop once it touches everywhere: the panel should still be at least 3/4" thick.
Flatten 1 this way.
mistakes: Holding the sander on a joint digs a hollow beside it. Keep the sander moving over a wide area.

safety.text: Breathing wood dust can cause respiratory symptoms. Wear a dust mask while you sand, and sweep up the dust rather than blowing it.
Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

Support the board on sawhorses or blocks on both sides of the cut, and clamp it.
technique: Mark the length and square a line across the face.
Hold the square tight to the edge, with the saw base against it and the blade on the waste side of the line.
Start the saw clear of the board and feed it through at an even speed.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Letting the saw drift away from the square bends the cut and can bind the blade. Keep the base tight to the square for the whole cut.

safety.text: A circular saw kicks back toward you when the blade pinches in the cut. Support the board and both pieces of it, so neither drops into the blade as the cut finishes, and keep your hands out of the line of the cut.

setup: Set the blade a little deeper than the board is thick, 3/4".
Support the board on sawhorses or blocks on both sides of the cut, and clamp it.
technique: Mark the length and square a line across the face.
Hold the square tight to the edge, with the saw base against it and the blade on the waste side of the line.
Start the saw clear of the board and feed it through at an even speed.
Cut 2 this way.
mistakes: Letting the saw drift away from the square bends the cut and can bind the blade. Keep the base tight to the square for the whole cut.

safety.text: A circular saw kicks back toward you when the blade pinches in the cut. Support the board and both pieces of it, so neither drops into the blade as the cut finishes, and keep your hands out of the line of the cut.

setup: Set the miter saw square, with no miter and no bevel.
Support the board level with the saw table on both sides of the blade.

Hold the board against the fence, with the blade on the waste side of the mark.
Let the blade reach full speed, then lower it through the board.
Let the blade stop before you raise it.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Cutting on the mark makes the part short by the width of the blade. Put the blade on the waste side of the mark.

steps.title: Cut the mortises

method.name: With a drill and a chisel

tools.use: a bit as wide as the mortise

setup: Mark the mortise on the part: 2-1/2" long and 1" wide, where the cut detail shows it.
Fit a bit 1" across, and mark it or set a stop for 2-1/2" deep.
Clamp the part flat, with the marked side up.
technique: Drill a row of holes inside the marks, each 2-1/2" deep, overlapping a little.
Pare the walls to the marks with the chisel, its flat side toward the wall and held upright.
Clean the bottom with the chisel until it is flat at 2-1/2" all along.
Check the fit with the tenon it holds, and pare where it binds.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Drilling at a lean makes the mortise wider at the bottom or out of line. Keep the bit upright, checking from two sides.
Prying with the chisel against a wall crushes the edge. Pare a little at a time, and lever only on the waste.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

setup: Fit a bit 3/4" across, and mark it or set a stop for 3/16" deep.
Clamp the part flat to the bench.
technique: Mark both walls of the dado and both of its ends, 15-3/16" apart.
Drill a row of holes inside the marks, each 3/16" deep, overlapping a little.
Pare the walls and ends to the marks with the chisel, its flat side toward the wall and held upright.
Pare the bottom flat at 3/16" all along.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Drilling at a lean makes the dado wider at the bottom or wanders off the line. Keep the bit upright, checking from two sides.

tools.use: a bit as wide as the dado

setup: Fit a bit 3/4" across, and mark it or set a stop for 3/16" deep.
Clamp the part flat to the bench.
technique: Mark both walls of the dado and both of its ends, 15-3/16" apart.
Drill a row of holes inside the marks, each 3/16" deep, overlapping a little.
Pare the walls and ends to the marks with the chisel, its flat side toward the wall and held upright.
Pare the bottom flat at 3/16" all along.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Drilling at a lean makes the dado wider at the bottom or wanders off the line. Keep the bit upright, checking from two sides.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

steps.title: Bore the hinge cups and drill the screw holes

method.name: With a drill/driver

tools.use: drilling pilot holes and driving the screws

setup: Mark each plate’s screw holes on the face from the cut detail.
Chuck a bit for the pilot holes, the size the hinge’s maker says for the plate’s screws.
technique: Drill a pilot hole at each mark, as deep as the screws go.
Set a plate on its marks the way the maker’s diagram shows, and drive its 2 screws until each head is snug.
Screw on 2 plates this way.
mistakes: A screw driven at full speed strips its hole in the side, and the plate works loose. Set the clutch low and drive the last turns slowly.
Setting a plate turned around puts the hinge’s arm on the wrong side. Check it against the maker’s diagram before driving.

safety.text: Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

suggestions.methodName: With a drill and an impact driver

method.name: With a drill
setup: Mark each hole where the cut detail shows it, and which ones are slots.
Fit a bit the screw slides through without threading into the wood: its clearance hole, as the screw maker gives it.
Clamp the part flat on scrap, so the bit comes out clean.
technique: Drill 2 round holes straight through the 1/2" part.
For each of the 0 slots, drill the first hole, then a second 0" beyond it the way the slot runs, and holes between them so they overlap.
Pare the sides of each slot straight with the chisel, so the screw slides from one end to the other.
Drill 2 this way.
mistakes: A slot run the wrong way stops the part from moving, which can split it. Check which way each slot runs before you drill.
Driving a screw in a slot tight pins the part. Turn it until it is snug, so its head can still slide.

steps.title: Fit the bench together dry

method.name: Without clamps
setup: Clear a flat surface big enough for the whole assembly, and have someone help hold the parts.
Lay the parts out in the order they go together, each with its marks facing the way the plan shows.
technique: Put the parts together without glue, sliding each one into its dadoes.
Push each joint closed by hand and look for a gap.
Measure both diagonals of the front. When they match, the assembly is square.
Mark where each part meets its neighbors, so it goes back the same way, then take it apart.
mistakes: Forcing a tight joint together dry can split a part or leave it stuck. Stop, take it apart, and widen the dado a little.
A joint held closed by hand can hide a gap that clamps would show. Check each one while it is pushed fully home.

anyOf: Clamps with widest opening at least 61-7/8" (you entered 24")

steps.title: Glue up the end frames

method.name: With clamps
setup: Dry-fit the assembly first, and have every part and clamp within reach: the glue starts to dry as soon as it is spread.
Open the clamps past 18-5/8", and cut scrap pads to go under the jaws so they do not dent the faces.
technique: Spread a thin, even coat of glue in each dado and on the part that goes into it.
Slide each part into its dadoes, and clamp across the assembly over each joint.
Tighten the clamps evenly until a small bead of glue squeezes out at each joint.
Measure both diagonals. If they differ, angle a clamp along the longer one and tighten it until they match.
Scrape off the squeezed-out glue once it turns rubbery, so it does not keep the finish out.
Leave the assembly clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
mistakes: Glue spread long before the parts go together dries on the wood and makes a thick, weak joint. Spread it on one joint group at a time and close it right away.
Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Taking the clamps off early lets the joints shift or open. Leave them on for as long as the glue maker says.

steps.title: Fit the drawer bottoms and fronts

method.name: With a drill/driver
setup: Set the parts in place and clamp them so they cannot shift while you drive the screws.
Set the driver’s clutch low, so it slips before a screw goes in too far.
technique: Drive each of the 9 screws through its hole until the head is snug against the wood.
Leave the screws in slots snug, not tight, so the part they hold can still slide.
mistakes: Driving a screw in a slot tight pins the part, which can split it as it moves. Stop when the head is snug.
A screw driven at full speed strips its hole. Drive the last turns slowly.

Forstner bits with deepest hole from one side at least 2-1/4"

method.name: With a drill, from one side
setup: Mark each hole center from the cut detail on the side you bore from.
Chuck a 3/4" bit, and clamp a scrap board tight under the part where the bit comes out.
technique: Stand a square on the part beside the bit, and bore through the 2-1/2" of wood, checking square from two directions as the bit starts.
Back the bit out every inch or so to clear the chips.
Bore 1 holes this way.
mistakes: Letting the drill tilt puts the hole off square, so what stands in it leans. Check square from two directions as the bit starts, and again halfway.
Pushing the bit out through the far face with nothing behind it tears out the wood around the hole. Clamp a scrap board tight behind it.

anyOf: Drill press with column to the center of the bit at least 1-3/4" and deepest hole in one stroke at least 5"

method.name: With a drill, from one side
setup: Mark each hole center from the cut detail on the side you bore from.
Chuck a 1-1/8" bit, and clamp a scrap board tight under the part where the bit comes out.
technique: Stand a square on the part beside the bit, and bore through the 2-1/2" of wood, checking square from two directions as the bit starts.
Back the bit out every inch or so to clear the chips.
Bore 1 holes this way.
mistakes: Letting the drill tilt puts the hole off square, so what stands in it leans. Check square from two directions as the bit starts, and again halfway.
Pushing the bit out through the far face with nothing behind it tears out the wood around the hole. Clamp a scrap board tight behind it.

steps.title: Ease the edges

method.name: With a sander
setup: Clamp the part flat, or hold it on a bench against a stop.
technique: Sand each long edge with the sander tilted, rolling it over the corner until the corner is round.
Round the corners at each end the same way.
Sand every face a hand can touch until no splinter catches on a rag drawn across it.
Ease 1 this way.
mistakes: Holding the sander in one place on an edge cuts a flat or a dip. Keep it moving along the whole edge.

steps.title: Finish

method.name: Sanded, then wiped on
setup: Choose the finish with an experienced builder, and read its instructions for coats, drying time, and ventilation.
Work where fresh air moves through, away from flames and heat.
technique: Sand every face a person can see or touch, with the grain, ending with finer paper than you started with.
Vacuum the dust, then wipe the faces with a clean cloth.
Wipe on a thin coat with a clean rag, then wipe off what has not soaked in, as the instructions say.
Let it dry as long as the instructions say, sand lightly with fine paper, and add as many coats as they call for.
mistakes: Sanding across the grain leaves scratches that the finish makes stand out. Sand with the grain.
A thick coat dries soft and sticky. Wipe on thin coats and wipe off the excess.

safety.text: Rags wet with oil-based finish can catch fire on their own. Store them in a tightly sealed metal container, then throw them away.

checklist.element: The base: legs, feet, and rails
checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the glued mortises and tenons keep the base square and steady when planing pushes the top along and across.
checklist.why: Hand planing pushes hard on a bench, and Kerf does not compute joint strength.

checklist.element: The bench with a vise open
checklist.confirm: Confirm whether the bench can tip when planing at an end past the legs, or with work in an open vise.
checklist.why: The top runs past the legs at each end, and a vise holds work farther out still.

checklist.element: The through tenons and the back mortises
checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder how much glue the front tenons through the top need, and that the back tenons stay unglued in their long mortises.
checklist.why: The top holds the frame together at its tenons, and gluing the back ones would stop it moving.

checklist.element: Glue lines in the top and legs
checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the strips of the top and legs are glued well enough for heavy work.
checklist.why: Kerf does not compute the strength of glue lines.

checklist.element: Bending and shear of the top
checklist.confirm: Confirm the top is strong enough, not only stiff enough.
checklist.why: There are no published design values for furniture lumber, so Kerf checks only deflection.

checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the dovetailed boxes suit what goes in them.
checklist.why: Tools are heavy, and Kerf computes nothing for the drawers.

steps.title: Let the lumber settle indoors

method.name: Stacked and left to settle
setup: Bring the boards into the room where the piece will stand, or a heated room like it, as soon as you buy them.
technique: Stack the boards flat with thin, dry strips of wood across them every foot or two, so air reaches every face.
Leave them for a couple of weeks before cutting, longer for boards that felt cool or damp at the store or that were stored outside.
mistakes: Gluing up boards that are still drying leaves them to shrink in the panel, which can open the joints or crack it. Give them time indoors first.
Stacking boards flat on each other traps moisture between them. Put strips between every layer.

steps.title: Let the lumber settle indoors

method.name: Stacked and left to settle
setup: Bring the boards into the room where the piece will stand, or a heated room like it, as soon as you buy them.
technique: Stack the boards flat with thin, dry strips of wood across them every foot or two, so air reaches every face.
Leave them for a couple of weeks before cutting, longer for boards that felt cool or damp at the store or that were stored outside.
mistakes: Gluing up boards that are still drying leaves them to shrink in the panel, which can open the joints or crack it. Give them time indoors first.
Stacking boards flat on each other traps moisture between them. Put strips between every layer.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the back legs' mortises, 3/16" longer toward the back, leave the top room to move against tenons glued at the front.
flags.why: The top moves across its 17-5/8" depth with the seasons, and the legs' tenons go through it 13-5/8" apart. The Wood Movement section estimates how much.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the 5" of top past the legs at each end carries heavy work there, such as chopping or work held in the end vise.
flags.why: Kerf computes only the top’s sag between the legs, not what it carries past them.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether screws for the upper drawers’ slides, driven into both faces of the divider at the same height, will meet inside it.
flags.why: Screws longer than half the divider’s 3/4" meet in the middle when the holes line up. Staggering the two slides’ holes, or shorter screws, avoids it.

steps.title: Cut board 1, a 13/16" x 5-1/2" 10' long: Top board for strips, Low rail board for strips

method.name: With a miter saw
setup: Set the miter saw square, with no miter and no bevel.
Support the board level with the saw table on both sides of the blade.
technique: Mark the length on the board.
Hold the board against the fence, with the blade on the waste side of the mark.
Let the blade reach full speed, then lower it through the board.
Let the blade stop before you raise it.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Cutting on the mark makes the part short by the width of the blade. Put the blade on the waste side of the mark.

safety.text: Keep the blade guard on and working: it must cover the blade whenever the blade is not in the wood.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

Support the board level with the saw table on both sides of the blade.
technique: Mark the length on the board.
Hold the board against the fence, with the blade on the waste side of the mark.
Let the blade reach full speed, then lower it through the board.
Let the blade stop before you raise it.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Cutting on the mark makes the part short by the width of the blade. Put the blade on the waste side of the mark.

safety.text: Keep the blade guard on and working: it must cover the blade whenever the blade is not in the wood.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

steps.title: Glue up the top, legs, and rails from strips

alternatives.methodName: With a band saw and a fence

method.name: In sections, with clamps and cauls
setup: Lay the 23 strips out in order, turned so the faces that meet are flat and clean, and mark a line across them so they go back the same way.
Clamp them dry to check that every glue line closes along its length with light pressure, and open the clamps past 18-11/16".
Cut straight scrap boards for cauls, as long as the glue-up is wide.
technique: Glue a few strips at a time into sections: spread glue evenly on every face that meets another, bring them together, and clamp them.

Put clamps along the length close enough together that a small bead of glue squeezes out along every glue line, alternating them on the two faces that show the strips’ edges, and clamp cauls across to hold the strips level.
Once a section’s glue holds, scrape off the squeeze-out on its faces, then glue the sections together the same way.
Leave the last glue-up clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
Glue up 1 this way.
mistakes: Spreading glue on every strip at once can take so long that the first faces dry before the clamps go on, and dried glue does not wet the other face. A section of a few strips goes together before that.
Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Strips that slip out of level leave a step on the edge faces deeper than flattening takes off. Keep the cauls tight and check each glue line with your fingers before the final tightening.

steps.title: Glue up the panels

method.name: With clamps and cauls
setup: Lay the 4 boards out in order with your marks lined up, and clamp them dry to check that every joint closes along its length with light pressure.
Open the clamps past 21-5/8", and cut straight scrap boards for cauls, as long as the panel is wide.
technique: Spread glue evenly along every glued edge.
Bring the boards together and put clamps across the panel, alternating above and below it.
Clamp a caul across each end of the panel, on both faces, to hold the boards level with each other.
Tighten the clamps evenly until a small bead of glue squeezes out along each joint.
Leave the panel clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
Glue up 1 this way.
mistakes: Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Using clamp pressure to close a gap leaves a thick, weak glue line. Joint the edges again until they meet along their length.
Glue left to skin over before the boards go together does not wet the other edge. Have everything ready before you spread the glue.

method.name: With a sander
setup: Let the panel rest for several days after glue-up, so the wood along the joints dries back before you sand it.
Scrape off the dried glue on both faces, and clamp the panel flat to the bench.
technique: Sand across each joint until the faces are level, then sand the whole face with the grain.
Check with a straightedge laid across the 21-5/8" panel as you go. Stop once it touches everywhere: the panel should still be at least 3/4" thick.
Flatten 1 this way.
mistakes: Holding the sander on a joint digs a hollow beside it. Keep the sander moving over a wide area.

safety.text: Breathing wood dust can cause respiratory symptoms. Wear a dust mask while you sand, and sweep up the dust rather than blowing it.
Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

method.name: With a circular saw, from two faces
setup: Set the blade as deep as it goes.
Support the board on sawhorses or blocks on both sides of the cut, and clamp it.
technique: Mark the length and square the line around all four faces.
Cut along the line on one face, with the blade on the waste side.
Turn the board over and cut along the line on the opposite face, so the two kerfs meet.

mistakes: Lines that do not meet at the corners leave a step where the two cuts meet. Square every line from the same edge and face, and check that the last line meets the first.

setup: Set the blade a little deeper than the board is thick, 1/2".
Support the board on both sides of the cut and clamp it.
technique: Mark 2-3/4" from the edge kept at both ends, and join the marks with a line.
Clamp a straight board along the line as a guide, set back by the distance from the blade to the edge of the saw base.
Keep the base tight to the guide and cut the full 22-13/16".
Rip 2 this way.
mistakes: A guide that is not straight puts its curve in the part. Sight along the guide board, or use a factory edge.

safety.text: A circular saw kicks back toward you when the blade pinches in the cut. Support the board and both pieces of it, so neither drops into the blade as the cut finishes, and keep your hands out of the line of the cut.

safety.text: Let the lower guard close over the blade on its own after every cut. Never wedge or tie it open.
Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.

Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

method.name: With a miter saw
setup: Set the miter saw square, with no miter and no bevel.
Support the board level with the saw table on both sides of the blade.
technique: Mark the length on the board.
Hold the board against the fence, with the blade on the waste side of the mark.
Let the blade reach full speed, then lower it through the board.
Let the blade stop before you raise it.

mistakes: Cutting on the mark makes the part short by the width of the blade. Put the blade on the waste side of the mark.

Support the board on sawhorses or blocks on both sides of the cut, and clamp it.
technique: Mark the length and square the line around all four faces.
Cut along the line on one face, with the blade on the waste side.
Turn the board over and cut along the line on the opposite face, so the two kerfs meet.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Lines that do not meet at the corners leave a step where the two cuts meet. Square every line from the same edge and face, and check that the last line meets the first.

safety.text: A circular saw kicks back toward you when the blade pinches in the cut. Support the board and both pieces of it, so neither drops into the blade as the cut finishes, and keep your hands out of the line of the cut.

Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

Support the board level with the saw table on both sides of the blade.

steps.title: Cut the mortises

method.name: With a drill and a chisel

tools.use: a bit as wide as the mortise

setup: Mark the mortise on the part: 2-1/2" long and 1" wide, where the cut detail shows it.
Fit a bit 1" across, and mark it or set a stop for 4" deep.
Clamp the part flat, with the marked side up.
technique: Drill a row of holes inside the marks, each 4" deep, overlapping a little.
Pare the walls to the marks with the chisel, its flat side toward the wall and held upright.
Clean the bottom with the chisel until it is flat at 4" all along.
Check the fit with the tenon it holds, and pare where it binds.
Cut 1 this way.
mistakes: Drilling at a lean makes the mortise wider at the bottom or out of line. Keep the bit upright, checking from two sides.
Prying with the chisel against a wall crushes the edge. Pare a little at a time, and lever only on the waste.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

steps.title: Bore the hinge cups and drill the screw holes

method.name: With a drill/driver

tools.use: drilling pilot holes and driving the screws

setup: Mark each plate’s screw holes on the face from the cut detail.
Chuck a bit for the pilot holes, the size the hinge’s maker says for the plate’s screws.
technique: Drill a pilot hole at each mark, as deep as the screws go.
Set a plate on its marks the way the maker’s diagram shows, and drive its 2 screws until each head is snug.
Screw on 2 plates this way.
mistakes: A screw driven at full speed strips its hole in the side, and the plate works loose. Set the clutch low and drive the last turns slowly.
Setting a plate turned around puts the hinge’s arm on the wrong side. Check it against the maker’s diagram before driving.

safety.text: Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

steps.title: Fit the bench together dry

method.name: Without clamps
setup: Clear a flat surface big enough for the whole assembly, and have someone help hold the parts.
Lay the parts out in the order they go together, each with its marks facing the way the plan shows.
technique: Put the parts together without glue, sliding each one into its dadoes.
Push each joint closed by hand and look for a gap.
Measure both diagonals of the front. When they match, the assembly is square.
Mark where each part meets its neighbors, so it goes back the same way, then take it apart.
mistakes: Forcing a tight joint together dry can split a part or leave it stuck. Stop, take it apart, and widen the dado a little.
A joint held closed by hand can hide a gap that clamps would show. Check each one while it is pushed fully home.

anyOf: Clamps with widest opening at least 61-7/8" (you entered 24")

steps.title: Glue up the end frames

method.name: With clamps
setup: Dry-fit the assembly first, and have every part and clamp within reach: the glue starts to dry as soon as it is spread.
Open the clamps past 18-5/8", and cut scrap pads to go under the jaws so they do not dent the faces.
technique: Spread a thin, even coat of glue in each dado and on the part that goes into it.
Slide each part into its dadoes, and clamp across the assembly over each joint.
Tighten the clamps evenly until a small bead of glue squeezes out at each joint.
Measure both diagonals. If they differ, angle a clamp along the longer one and tighten it until they match.
Scrape off the squeezed-out glue once it turns rubbery, so it does not keep the finish out.
Leave the assembly clamped for as long as the glue maker says.
mistakes: Glue spread long before the parts go together dries on the wood and makes a thick, weak joint. Spread it on one joint group at a time and close it right away.
Clamping as hard as you can squeezes out the glue the joint needs. Tighten only until a small, even bead appears.
Taking the clamps off early lets the joints shift or open. Leave them on for as long as the glue maker says.

method.name: With a drill, from one side
setup: Mark each hole center from the cut detail on the side you bore from.
Chuck a 3/4" bit, and clamp a scrap board tight under the part where the bit comes out.
technique: Stand a square on the part beside the bit, and bore through the 4" of wood, checking square from two directions as the bit starts.
Back the bit out every inch or so to clear the chips.
Bore 1 holes this way.
mistakes: Letting the drill tilt puts the hole off square, so what stands in it leans. Check square from two directions as the bit starts, and again halfway.
Pushing the bit out through the far face with nothing behind it tears out the wood around the hole. Clamp a scrap board tight behind it.

mistakes: Holding the sander in one place on an edge cuts a flat or a dip. Keep it moving along the whole edge.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the preservative in your treated lumber calls for more than a dust mask, gloves, and washing up when you sand it.
flags.why: Breathing wood dust can cause allergic and other respiratory symptoms, and dust from treated wood carries the preservative.

steps.title: Finish

method.name: Sanded, then wiped on
setup: Choose the finish with an experienced builder, and read its instructions for coats, drying time, and ventilation.
Work where fresh air moves through, away from flames and heat.
technique: Sand every face a person can see or touch, with the grain, ending with finer paper than you started with.
Vacuum the dust, then wipe the faces with a clean cloth.
Wipe on a thin coat with a clean rag, then wipe off what has not soaked in, as the instructions say.
Let it dry as long as the instructions say, sand lightly with fine paper, and add as many coats as they call for.
mistakes: Sanding across the grain leaves scratches that the finish makes stand out. Sand with the grain.
A thick coat dries soft and sticky. Wipe on thin coats and wipe off the excess.

safety.text: Rags wet with oil-based finish can catch fire on their own. Store them in a tightly sealed metal container, then throw them away.
Breathing wood dust can cause respiratory symptoms. Wear a dust mask while you sand, and sweep up the dust rather than blowing it.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

sources.locator: Purpose, p. 1, and Power tools, general precautions, p. 4

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder which finish suits the wood and where it will stand, and follow the product's instructions for ventilation.
flags.why: Rags wet with oil-based finish can catch fire on their own. Store them in a tightly sealed metal container, then throw them away.
